Bessie Coleman. The aviator who became the first Black woman to earn a pilot's license. On her path to breaking barriers, Coleman faced discrimination from both racial and gender perspectives in an industry dominated by white men. To pursue aviation, she learned French so she could attend flight school in France, where racial discrimination was less pervasive than in the United States. In 1921, she earned her pilot's license from the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale. She worked as a stunt pilot and barnstormer, performing aerial shows and demonstrations across the country. Coleman never realized her dream of opening a flight school for African Americans. In 1926, while performing in an aeronautical show in Jacksonville, Florida, she died in an accident during a test flight. Her legacy lay dormant for decades before eventually being reclaimed and recognized. Today, Coleman stands as a pioneer, breaking through racial and gender barriers in aviation's earliest days. Amelia Earhart, who came later, also broke gender barriers in aviation, though she had far greater resources and recognition than Coleman ever did.
